newsitem.title: INDIA: Socialists threaten to quit India ruling alliance.
newsitem.headline: Socialists threaten to quit India ruling alliance.

text.p: A key socialist group threatened on Tuesday to pull out of India's centre-left government if Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda backed a rival party's claim to rule the country's most populous state. Opinion polls have predicted a hung assembly in Uttar Pradesh state, where local elections end this week.
Voting for five remaining seats in the 425-member assembly was set for Wednesday.
Ballot counting in the state of 140 million people was set to begin on Wednesday, and a clear picture of party strengths was expected by late Thursday, officials said.

The polls are considered crucial because Deve Gowda's United Front is pitted against both the main opposition Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and the Congress party, which offers make-or-break backing to Deve Gowda in the federal parliament.
The Hindu nationalist BJP is widely tipped to emerge as the largest group with an outside chance of forming a government.
Defence Minister Mulayam Singh Yadav's socialist Samajwadi Party is the main arm of Deve Gowda's fractious United Front alliance in Uttar Pradesh.

Deve Gowda wants to block the BJP's bid for state power. To do so, he would need the support of a local alliance linking former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao's Congress party and the low-caste Hindu Bahujan Samajwadi Party (BSP).
Congress has told Deve Gowda to back BSP leader Mayawati for the state chief minister's job. The Samajwadi Party sees the demand as undermining Yadav's drive to become chief minister.
But United Front leaders from outside Yadav's Samajwadi Party said they would not rule out any alliance to keep out the BJP, including supporting Mayawati.

"If there is any move to weaken Malayam Singh, then we will not remain in the government," Samajwadi Party spokesman and Communications Minister Beni Prasad Varma told Reuters in the state capital Lucknow.

"Much as we respect Mr Deve Gowda, we will not allow anyone to humiliate us in our own state," Varma said when asked if Yadav would allow Mayawati to become chief minister. He said under no circumstances would the Samajwadi Party back Mayawati.
Politicians said Deve Gowda's problems were compounded by a bitter quarrel between Mayawati and Yadav, a former chief minister.

Mayawati had backed Yadav's government until last year when she withdrew her support to become chief minister with the BJP's backing. The alliance of convenience collapsed after four months and New Delhi imposed direct rule over the sprawling northern state.

An opinion poll this week in India Today magazine predicted between 116 to 132 assembly seats for the Samajwadi Party-led United Front. It gave the BSP-Congress alliance between 80 and 95 seats, against 185 to 205 for the BJP.
Any ruling group would need 213 members for a simple majority in the state assembly.
Congress state President Jitendra Prasada said his party would not support Yadav as chief minister.
"We have supported the Deve Gowda government in Delhi," Prasada told Reuters. "It is only logical that they support our alliance in Uttar Pradesh."
Deve Gowda wants Congress, whose 140 deputies shore up his government against the BJP's unceasing challenge in the federal parliament, to join his coalition in New Delhi.
His discreet efforts to woo Congress members in New Delhi have been criticised by communists, who see Congress as their main rival in their leftist bastions of West Bengal and Kerala states.
Mayawati told Reuters that if the Congress joins Deve Gowda's government, her BSP deputies would also support him.
"It doesn't really remain important then to keep Mulayam Singh in the (federal) government," she said.
